game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I really wanted to give this a positive review, as someone who loves games like this ( Papers Please! being a personal favorite)

However, I'm very indifferent due to the lack of content and the seemingly linear focus of the story and the severe lack of challenge ( all your options are highlighted for you)

It had a TON of potential and did give a very 1984ish vibe, and I enjoyed the small amounts of content it offered ( 30 minutes an episode?). However if you, like me, go into this expecting a Papers Please! experience you will be severely disappointed.

5/10 ( don't buy unless it is on sale is my reccomendation -- or until all episodes have been unlocked for one continuous playthrough)

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What a wasted opportunity.

I went into this game wanting to like it - I really did. To be clear - I played through the entire game, finishing each of the 5 chapters.

Orwell is ostensibly a game about a surveillance state gone terribly wrong - but almost at every opportunity, it fails to make any meaningful point and constantly gets in its own way.

It starts bad. Rather than giving you, as a player, the agency to incriminate and potentially ruin the lives of the people you are surveilling, the game immediately puts you at arms-length. You are nothing more than a data collector with the ability to find and store information, but not make any meaningful analysis or conclusions about this data. Worse, it pairs you with the clumsily-written and drearily heavy-handed Symes - the *actual* investigator, who acts on the information you upload and is a constant source of awkward, immersion-breaking, and stupid commentary. 

It's true that, in principle, the data you choose to upload can affect the lives and outcomes of the people whose privacy you're invading - the trouble is that there's no real incentive to do so. Oftentimes, you must upload certain pieces of data in order to move the story along - which makes sense, because you're nothing more than a glorified data monkey clicking blue text and throwing it into a database. If you choose to hide a piece of information, it's not clear whether or not you'll be able to progress through the story. If you get something wrong (in the extremely limited range of things you are even allowed to get wrong), there are few consequences - an issue exacerbated by how distanced you are from everything that goes down. You don't really get to make the call, figure out the deduction, or even choose whether or not you should be wielding the awesome power you do. You either progress the story, or you don't - Symes is the one who gets to actually decide.

What's worse is that each of the characters in the game are utterly unlikable - the crimes you investigate them for are legitimate crimes that hurt real innocents and pose genuine dangers to the society in which they inhabit - the moral quandary that this game should so naturally lend itself to (the invasion of privacy, the loss of intimacy, that everybody is a criminal under mass surveillance, etc.,) is utterly and absolutely wasted. Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance.

Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue.

At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. 

Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. 

Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. 

Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary.

By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience.

Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. 

I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game.

Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful.

This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Pros:
- Art style is interesting and engaging
- Story is well crafted and immersive
- Exposition isn't forced on you, but it is there if you wish to learn more about the world or certain characters
- Creators clearly spent a lot of time and effort on the setting 
- The game tackles some pretty engaging ethical dilemas that are applicable to the world we live in

Cons:
- Click and drag simulator 2016
- Uninspired gameplay mechanics 
- Constant handholding (I kept thinking I was in a long tutorial but that's just how the game is)
- Very binary choices (he did it vs she did it/ she did the right thing vs she is bad)
- No real detective work the game just tells you everything
- The game treats you like an idiot by having a sidekick tell you what each piece of info means


Other things that bothered me:

-      Chat/phone calls move too fast to keep up with uploading the 'chunks' that appear and you're forced to either ignore the dialogue progression and try to click on a certain chuck as the screen constantly shifts or wait until the exchange is  done to upload anything (or maybe I was just too slow).

-      Music shifts in tone dramtically whenever 'shocking info' is revealed which makes the game feel very linear (which it is) instead of just letting you stumble upon the info yourself and make your own conclusions as to what is important. The music changes give the feeling of "This was a scripted event that I experienced at a designated time."

-      Your partner/boss just tells you things so you don't really have to do any investigation yourself which is kind the whole point of the game. 

-      You are fed information in a pretty constant chronological stream instead being given all the info at once and having to sort through it with your brain. The game treats you like a baby and doesn't give you your next treat until you click and drag the things on the page it just gave you. 

-      The game established this rhythm really early of scrolling through a page, clicking on stuff, listening to your buddy pal guy tell you stuff, being given a new page, then repeating.

-      The fact that the chats/calls don't start until you actively bring them up is quite harmful to immersion (why would the people wait to start talking on the phone for 5 seconds until I'm monitoring them? Just have them act like normal humans and not wait for the player).

-      The gameplay would be a lot better if the events driving the characters weren't so close to the present. If we as players were given this new technology to help solve a crime in the past (several months at least) it would eliminate the need to have these awfully convenient text conversations and phone calls every 5 seconds that always have important info. What I'm saying is put the event in the past so that the player can be given a bunch of call transcripts and chat logs to sift through instead of being handed the info.

-      The very nature of how the game highlights all of the important info for you makes you question what your job really is and why anyone would need you to do it. If they already have a system that determines what is important and human operators who interpret the data (your boss/partner guy), why the hell do they need you???

-      The info highlighting eventually has you just scrolling through pages until something lights up or you get an update instead of actually reading the page and deciding what is important and what is irrelevant.




This is not a bad game by any means. It's just always frustrating when I see one of these "choices matter" games where there's clearly a certain path you're encouraged to take and you really aren't free to do things your own way.

While I had pretty high expectations for this game after coming off a Hacknet binge, I just feel as though the game is trying to pretend to be something it's not. Just market the game for what it is, a linear narrative experience.

I'm very aware that since I did not finish the game my perspective is limited to what I played, but what I played I did not enjoy, so I cannot reccomend this game.

TL;DR: This game is a very and hand-holdy linear story based experience while it is advertised to be a sort of detective

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Intresting premise,  poor execution. In the attempt to create stakes for the players decision, Orwell goes out of it's way to obfuscate or even fail to present clarfying information until after the decision is made. It also prevents refinement of past data with new context. Being forced to compete in the 20 meter jump to conclusions in order to find the context you needed to make that conclusion is beyond obxnoxious. This is made worse by there being minimal clarity to what the data you've supplied will be intreperted as, and that intreptation is final with little abitliy to recontextualize. 

This of course undermines any moral arguement the game attempts to present or have you consider. Over surveillance, the effect of technology on the governments ability to monitor it's citizens and so forth are good topics to explore. However demonstarting the conquences by forcing the player to pick up the idiot ball does no one any favours.  

The concept is good, if you can deal with being forced to make uncontextualized leaps of judgement you might enjoy the game. But the inability to use good inquirial practices like preserving and rexamining conflicting data in light of new evidence kills the game for me.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Drag-and-Drop Simulator. Interactive story at best - not much for a point-and-click adventure.

Owell isn't the first "surveillance sim", and certainly isn't the best. It does plenty of things right, but far more wrong. Because of that, while I enjoyed the game and didn't feel the gameplay bad - I can't recommend it. 

The game holds your hand literally the entire way. It highlights information. It tells you when you've looked over a document and missed something. It repeats the obvious to you via your "advisor", Symes. It doesn't encourage reading whatsoever despite it only having pros as an interactive story.

One of the most irritating things of the game was Symes. Symes is your advisor through the game, commenting on evidence you find. The problem is that he comments on Ever. Little. Piece. of evidence. If you add someone's favorite color - Symes chimes in. If you add a new profile picture for a person - he has something SO IMPORTANT to say that it stops gameplay until you click continue. Again and again and again. 

Other elements of the game leave you wishing you were more in control of the program. For example, I wanted the ability to create profiles on people but you aren't given that permission. Symes gives you permission when you reach a certain point in the story, and that's that. I wanted to add a profile picture for someone I had a profile on..... NOPE couldn't do it until the game gives you permission to.

The game really gives you the illusion of control while the entire time you are limited to dragging and dropping story elements. The conflicts in data are VERY minor and ultimately the story wraps up in a similar way either way. It's the feeling of diverse while being completely linear. In the instances where there WERE conflicts in data, you really have to take a shot in the dark sometimes. 

So what did I expect? I wanted to be in charge of the note taking! I wanted to be able to create profiles on my own. I didn't want information to get highlighted for me UNLESS there was a problem. I wanted to be able to figure things out the entire time without some doofus interrupting gameplay the entire time with his commentary (Symes). 

Still, there are certainly pros to give this game. The story is interesting, the graphics are BEAUTIFUL for the genre, and the point-and-click adventure feel is definitely there, even if the game leads you where you need to go. Browse websites and news articles as though you were in your very own web browser! Now that I say that in writing, it doesn't seem all that impressive, but it's still enjoyable. The "accessing computer" elements and phone conversation elements I enjoy so much more than the web browsing.

All in all, it's an interesting point-and-click interactive story with multiple outcomes. It's not a difficult one, and there are no puzzles to solve, so just sit back and enjoy it. I still can't recommend it to anyone who is a fan of hacksims, surveillance sims, or information gathering sims though.... this is an interactive story - nothing more. It's no more "investigatory" than any of the TellTale games.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Interesting, compelling, and flawed. Contrary to some negative reviews I don't mind the format of Orwell being a linear visual novel, sometimes the best way to tell a complicated story is to tell it simply, and for what it's worth, it works well as long as Orwell is telling the story it thinks it is. 

With that being said, Orwell pulls its biggest punch on its lynchpin issue concerning its closing question on a terrorist attack you've been investigating from the beginning of the story, where, when circling back at the climax, Orwell thinks it's asking you a sensible question. Would I condemn the use of Orwellian nation state surveillance in the face of what we've learned during the story? 

Of course it's something I condemn, we've all a right to privacy.

But in order to answer the question as Orwell wants to phrase it, i found myself being really frustrated with how the game allows you to give your answer, and i'm really disappointed with what feels like really negligent storytelling. 

Orwell isnt as mature as it thinks it is. At the crux of it, Orwell isn't asking you to measure freedom against safety, It asks would you rather be a bootlicker to solve a terror attack killing several and wounding others, or let the perpetrators off because the developers skipped watching minority report?

We've a right to live free from terror, and the real fault of Orwell is that it ends up presenting terror and surveillance as equivalent issues rather than being in tension with one another. You're not asked what would you be willing to do to prevent an act of terror, it's already happened, people have died.

That Orwell also asks if you would like to give the system a middle finger by way of a Watergate sidestep to, again, apprehending conspirators / co-conspirators to a terror attack seems to be completely missing the point.

Am I missing things and details here? Almost certainly, there are a few different endings and granular differences depending on your choices throughout the story that paint a different picture. But for me, Orwell treats 1984 as the only book on the shelf.

The idea of playing an investigator using a dystopian surveillance system is genuinely intriguing, and it did pull me in at first. But in my case, a few elements caught me off guard, and I ultimately landed on the feeling of, “Damn, this could have been great.”

You're heavily railroaded. A handler constantly directs you, and you're only allowed to submit pre-highlighted data. So even if you spot something meaningful, if it hasn’t been highlighted, it’s off-limits… unless the system decides to highlight it later. In other words, it's Orwell—not your judgment—deciding what's relevant and when.
Also, can’t look into unimportant connections, people connected to the main people you’re already watching. That undermines immersion. Information and connections that should enrich the world instead feel like empty filler, like walking through a map where only the area around your destination actually exists. It undercuts the immersion hard, and it really starts to highlight how little control the player has over the investigation. The joy of organizing fragmented data and piecing together insight, the detective puzzle vibe you’d expect, is barely there.

Even the surveillance state itself feels oddly toothless. Orwell is supposedly a powerful system, yet the most basic info must be found manually. I get that the in-game incident is Orwell's first mission, but if the game is trying to sell a functioning surveillance state, it comes off half-baked.
Starting the investigation from scratch, with no basic personal data preloaded, makes the process resemble ordinary police work more than the operation of a dystopian digital panopticon.

The system’s invasive abilities (like tapping calls or accessing private devices without consent) do hint at Orwell’s dystopian cruelty. But from the player’s point of view, Orwell never allows unrestricted monitoring. Only designated “persons of interest” can be investigated, and since the events revolve around terrorism with real casualties, even the more questionable actions can be framed as emergency measures. This waters down the ethical tension; Orwell’s moral horror feels too easy to rationalize.
Even when one character challenges the legitimacy of Orwell’s power, their argument rings hollow—coming from someone involved in a bombing, it’s hard to see them as anything other than a villain delivering a monologue.

And when the second half of the game shows [spoiler]people casually messing stuff up[/spoiler], it makes you wonder: maybe the surveillance wasn’t that tight to begin with? How effective is this Orwell network if [spoiler]people willing to say "f*ck the system" and can still go full riot mode[/spoiler]? If the system’s that fragile, then what was the point of its supposed success in lowering crime in the first place?
I couldn’t quite tell whether this game was trying to criticize the dystopia built around Orwell or somehow justify it.

Also, you can’t skip or fast-forward dialogue, which I get is supposed to simulate “real-time surveillance,” but it just kills the pacing. This took me about four hours to get through the all chapters, and the lack of any way to redo choices just makes the idea of replaying for achievements or alternate paths a hard no.

ディストピアの監視システムを用いる調査官という導入は凄く面白いし実際に惹き込まれましたが、幾つかの要素が引っ掛かって最終的に「惜しいな」という感想に着地しました。

有り体に言うと意外と(?)自由度が低い。プレイヤーが進行の主導権を握っていないというのが率直な感想です。
まずアドバイザーが就くので情報の海に放り出されて手探りで進むのではなく自然と一本道になるので未知の間を自走する楽しみが希薄です。
更に、二次的な関係者(直接の監視対象ではない人々)の情報には触れられず、例えば誰かの両親や友人等が相関図に載っても飽くまで賑やかしで、RPGで言うなら「目的地周辺だけ作ってあるマップ」みたいな印象を受けるので没入感を削がれます。
そしてOrwellでは“ハイライトされている情報だけ”が利用可能なのですが、例えば関係者の画像を見付けたから登録したいと思ってもハイライトされていないなら使えない――と思いきや後になって急にハイライトされるという事も。つまりシステム(進行度等)の都合で意味の有無が一転してしまうので「役に立つか分からないが留めておきたい」みたいな遊び方は全く想定されておらず、“調査官”という言葉から連想して捜査・整理・推理というパズル的な喜びを期待すると肩透かしを食らいます。

物語や世界観についても引っ掛かります。国民の情報がOrwellに登録されておらず、住所も電話番号も全てプレイヤーが探し出す事になるのは、ゲーム内での事案がOrwellの初陣であるにせよ監視社会のディストピアを念頭に置くなら中途半端な気がしますし、基本的な個人情報から調査となると手順に警察の捜査との差異も感じられません。
Orwellを通じた通話や情報端末への無許可でのアクセスは人権や倫理への一種の加害性というディストピアがディストピアたる所以を描写してはいますが、プレイヤーの視点では上記の通り(=重要人物以外には触れられない) 犯罪や危機の捜査にしか使われておらず、しかも問題となる事件が死傷者を伴うテロなので、倫理観を脇に置くのは超法規的措置だと補完する事も出来てしまう。
その犯人がOrwellを非難したところで犠牲者を生んだテロリストの言説として空虚に響くだけでしょう。
また[spoiler]後半での展開も炎上からの破壊行動が容易く起きるのなら[/spoiler]“監視”の程度も大した事はないのでは？と感じます。監視なんぞ知るかという人が[spoiler]暴徒化したのだとしたら[/spoiler]、そもそも犯罪率の低下とは何だったんでしょうか。
正直なところ、この作品がOrwellに在る社会構造を否定的に描いているのか肯定的に描いているのか判然としませんでした。

実績や細かい分岐の確認に改めてプレイしていたら印象も変わるのかもしれませんが、ここでシステム面が障害に。というのも、だいぶのんびりしたプレイで全5章終わらせるのに約4時間掛かったのですが、Orwellには台詞送りやスキップ機能がなく、更には選択に修正が効かない仕様なのでリプレイへの精神的なハードルが高いです。
台詞送りやスキップが無いのはリアルタイムの盗聴という表現であるにしても快適性を損ないますし、こういった部分も作品の魅力を自ら削いでいる様な感じがしてなりません。

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The problem I have with this game is that it tries to hold you accountable for choices you did not make. Your task in Orwell is simply to retrieve information, someone will make a decision based on the information you collect. However, you are not in control of when this person makes a decision, so at times your attempt to gather all information to get the full picture are halted midway.  In addition, you are forced to choose between information chunks at crucial moments in the game even though there is no reason why you should. By doing so, the game forces you to not consider the entire context. And what does the game do to you at end? Blame you for not considering the entire context.

Another problem I have with this game is the more philosophical debate of an Orwellian surveillance system. By pretending that there is no separation of power or strict legislation on how evidence may be gathered, the creators abuse the fictive setting to criticize such a system. Yes, such a system would be horrible in certain dictatorship countries that currently exist, but we already know that don't we? It's an interesting concept that can be used for good as well. This nuance is missing in the story and as a result the writers and this game discredit themselves as a worthy piece of fiction.

The only thing I have found nice in this game is the interface. Aside from that, there is little meat around the bone.

I've seen free games on Kongregate that are longer to finish than this game. Also, it's another of these incompleted games that comes into chapters... I mean come on! This ain't a graphic-based game, surely you can publish a complete game... it's just text damnit! I know games in the 1980s that were deeper than this!

Where is the gaming industry heading anyways with such tiny games? Make this thing free. If I can get bigger better games for free, why should I pay for this?

It seems linear, at least I did not see any changes... reminds me of The Walking Dead series minus the interactions.

I cannot recommend this "game" until it is finished and takes as much time as it costs in dollars in hours. Right now, should be 8 hours of gameplay but it's like 30-45min of gameplay (that's what it took me to finish both chapters... very very short chapters... I mean my 10 pages short story is longer than this).

I,ve asked for a refund. My thematic boardgame prototype has more text, depth and replayability than this computer game, I am not even paid to do it.

Don't buy until the full game is here otherwise you will be disappointed with this 30 min game... go play free games on Kongregate instead, much more fun and cheaper.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I really wish I liked it because on the paper it's 100% a game for me but I'm forced to admit I just don't.

First of all it's not detective work, you just drop pieces of information in a database hoping it makes the story progress.

Because you're not technically forced to drop all the information in the database, you quickly try to have an impact on the story's progression by keeping some info to yourself, but the story only progresses when specific info is used and you never know which info is necessary or not so you can't really make informed choices on what to give Orwell and what to not.

I quickly find myself stuck with the story not progressing because I've decided to keep a piece of information that's mandatory for the story to continue and so I have to start from the top and review everything which is tedious and drop random bits of information I've kept until I find the one that was necessary for the story to continue which means I really can't choose what I keep or don't keep,

or I straight up give all the info away from the start to not have to review everything later once I'm stuck which again means I can't choose what I keep or don't keep.

There seems to be a system of highlighting the files where there still is relevant information but I don't understand how it works. Sometimes files are highlighted and there's nothing left on them and sometimes they aren't highlighted and there's still important things on them. It's very confusing.

I also suspect the political messaging of the game is really not so subtle and just "violence is bad" with no nuance but I can't tell you for sure because I'm too frustrated with the gameplay to go to the end of the story at this point. My other issue with the writing that I just can't seem to get over is that it makes zero sense that people who are fighting surveillance would post on the internet about it with their full name and photo or extremely basic aliases. Not posting about your actions on the internet is activism 101.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a game that I have mixed feeling about. While I did enjoy the game, I also want to clarify that there is certainly more than one issue with the game that makes me want to not recommend it.

The gameplay boils down to one and only one mechanic. Being able to drag selected text into a profile which affects the story. You need to bounce between internet pages, phone-call logs, and a few other forms of data to find keywords and important text to upload. Depending on what you upload, what the government believes and what happens to the person(s) involved changes. Do you portray a spoiled brat as a terrorist? An old man as a kind teacher. You decide what information they've put online defines them, very literally. 

The issues I have with this is as such: 
[olist]
    [*]Choices don't ultimately matter.
    [*]It is painfully short.
    [*]A lack of any audio design.
[/olist]

From top to bottom, the linearity of the game. Despite being able to chose what information does or doesn't get uploaded, a lot (and I do mean a LOT) of events will happen regardless of your actions. The game literally says in it's description: "But, be warned, the information you supply will have consequences." However, despite this, the only things my choices ended up affecting were the achievements. And spoiler alert: [spoiler] You can get any of the three endings no matter what choices you made in previous episodes. [/spoiler] Sure, on a superficial surface level your choices have consequences, but these "consequences" never actually impact your story or gameplay expericence.

Onto the next, the length. You may see me having 7.5 hours and tell me "Oh well 7.5 hours in NOT a short game!" You'd be right. Except Orwell is not 7.5 hours long, it is 3 hours long at most and 2 hours long at it's shortest. The only reason I have more than 3 hours of playtime is because I went back to get all of the achievements, which is also why i know how little your choices affect the story. I've seen all the endings, seen the affect of almost all of the choices, and even then with some time spent idle I was able to see 99% of this game's offerings in under 8 hours. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought the game on sale for 8€ and finished the story within 4hrs.

Pros:

+Important and contemporary message in the light of NSA scandals and the demise of privacy in general.
+Choice matters
+Original gameplay offers a new take on the genre of text adventures.
+Nice interface
+Unique design


Cons:

-The hacking and surveilance parts are way off. In a game like this I would've hoped for more realism.
-Even though choice matters you're being guided by your supervisor in the game. You can withhold information from him but whenever I felt like doing that it was a piece of information mandatory for the story to continue. At 2-way story-forks the most interesting option often was missing I felt, which again lead to the feeling of being railroaded.
-Almost every bit of information you put into the system is commented by a pop-up comment of your supervisor which becomes a nuisance rather quickly.


Conclusion:

I really wanted to like this game. The theme of George Orwells "1984" is more relevant than ever. However I feel like the games tries too hard to hammer home their point of everybody being "frameable" by using one unforseeable plot-twist after another, which again is due to the supervisor railroading you. Also I would rather pay like 5€ more and have the tapped phone calls be actual phone calls instead of reading through live transcipts.

Meh.

Positively meh.  I'll be honest, I played the game for a little while and then went and read a bunch of reviews about it, and I realized that this game definitely is not for me.  At the end of the day, the concept reeled me in, but the game failed to deliver nearly as much as I thought it would.  Things are a little bit too straight forward, and there is not nearly enough depth.  Also, for as much as the game pretends that you can choose some information and ignore others, it simply isn't true.  In the early game especially, you can hit a dead end if you choose to ignore certain information, and the game does not give you any indication that there is nothing more you can do.  I wish the game would tell you when you HAD TO DO something in order to proceed.  And then, in that vein, it feels like you are playing a rail-shooter, replaced with just clicking-and-dragging information.

Worth checking out if you can get it for free or less than a dollar, but otherwise, there are probably better games you can pass your time with.  Your mileage may vary.

review_text_raw:
Here's what happens: You get told to look up this woman who may have commited a crime. You don't actually look up anything, you just click on the page it gives you. It highlights what in that page you are supposed to save. It tells you when you have collected all of the information from that page and moves on to the next one. The entire game is just looking at these pages, or conversations, and dragging highlighted text or photos to a folder. That's it.
This game doesn't require thinking, not really. I thought the fact that you could choose what text you send over meant you could omit anything you wanted, but then it won't move on to the next series of pages. You have to send it something, and it pretty much all leads to the same outcomes.
It could have been a lot better. If it wasn't so linear, if you were left to search and find things on your own, if you could pick out which people to build a dossier on, anything like that would have made this awesome.

review_text_raw:
I hesitated before giving the thumb down to a game which is not completely bad, but definitely not for everyone.
The game basically plays like a visual story where you have to grab (drag  & drop more exactly) chunks of data to the left of the screen on the right character, the interface is not perfect (no right clicking to add intel faster, some back buttons are just visuals). The game is SLOW and a bit boring if you play in one go, no way to speed up text, no voice acting, forces you to wait on a few occasions. 
The writing isn't bad but characters lack personnality (bit shallow, not enough background), the game forces you to go one way and lacks some imaginative gameplay (older games would have make you work with visual clues, make interrogation yourself but Orwell keeps making you reading text). The problem is that it plays like a slow VN where you have to constantly look for the next button without any way to speed things up. 
It's not overly long but it feels long and the whole debate it's supposed to bring up falls a bit flat, also you can guess the "responsible person" before the end as soon as some intel is revealed. 
The game offers several ends but does not warn you before making the final choice (it did force you to watch a wall of text on an ugly colored screen before though) and would force you to replay from scratch to make another choice.

Don't mistaken me, those who are in for a lengthy text experience set in the modern world with text centered spying are in for a treat but it's definitely not for everyone.

Okay... I don't usually write game reviews. I generally have a pretty good idea of what I'm buying beforehand on Steam, and if a game is shit it's usually because I paid for shit. But this fucking game got me.

The biggest trick is that little "Choice Matters" tag that people gave it. I love choice games. The replay value of finding every unique ending alone usually makes it worth the price. There's also something thrilling, something special to video games, when you're able to make a choice and know it matters.

Choice doesn't matter in this game.

You do ultimately get to choose what's "shown" to your supervisor, and sometimes those choices do affect the game in some way. But you're railroaded HARD through just about every major event, forced to fight for even the smallest change in dialogue from game to game. The only half-consequential "choice" you get comes at the end, and to get there you need to sit through 2+ hours of the exact same gameplay. You might as well be buying the game to play once. If you're ok with playing once and then quitting (the game does have some beautiful artwork and some really gripping moments) then by all means do so. But if you want your choices to really matter, don't buy Orwell.

Long story short: Great interactive [b]novel[/b]. Very addicting and compelling storytelling.

Long story ahead:
But, is this a game? And if it is a game what is the [i]enjoyment[/i] a player could have from playing it?

I have three main references as game definition:
[list]
[*][quote]Games are an exercise of voluntary control systems, in which there is a contest between powers, confined by rules in order to produce a disequilibrial outcome.
—Elliot Avedon and Brian Sutton-Smith[/quote]
[*][quote]A game is an interactive structure of endogenous meaning that requires players to struggle toward a goal.
—Greg Costikyan[/quote]
[*][quote]
A game is a closed, formal system, that engages players in structured conflict, and resolves in an unequal outcome.
—Tracy Fullerton, Chris Swain, and Steven Hoffman[/quote]
[/list]
Maybe you are questioning yourself why should I to struggle to classify Orwell as a game or as an interactive novel. The reply is really simple: because it changes a lot the review. And just because Orwell is very borderline I will review it twice, one review as an interactive novel and one as a game letting the reader to choose what fits best.

[b]Orwell as an interactive graphic novel[/b]
The story is really interesting and compelling, keeping you addicted to it until the end.

The novel is [i]pretty short[/i], I have walkthrough it twice in less than 11 hours, but when the storytelling is strong, able to immerse the reader, shortness is not an issue.

The music is nice, but a bit [i]repetitive[/i], above all when you hear mostly the same loop for hours, broken for short time by a drama loop.

Maybe this interactive novel is a bit too much expensive, but it is strongly suggested if you are able to get it on sale.


[b]Orwell as a game[/b]
Pros:
[list]
[*]Story
[/list]
Cons:
[list]
[*]Lack of choice and freedom
[*]Event based system and strong linear game, if you don't do what is expected the story does not go on
[*]Less than 8 hours of gameplay to get to the end (first time you play, otherwise a lot less)
[*]Max of 3-4 replays before having seen all what the game has to offer meaning less than 20/25 hours of total gameplay.

[/list]

I am sorry but being this sold as a game I couldn't [b]honestly[/b] suggest to buy it, and anyway as I have already written as an interactive novel is a bit too much expensive.

- Music is OK
- The characters are relatable
- Story is realistic
- This implementation of mass surveillance is plausible

- Lack of immersion stemming from weak game mechanics.

- The web is way too small, and computer hacking is way too minimalistic to be plausible.
- The enjoyment as you progress is almost a total downward slope. I think the last episode and the ending is just not ready.
- Game lasts no more than 8 hours.

review_text_raw:
Orwell is a "profession simulator" style interactive novel where you control a privacy invading government employee, reading peoples emails and watching security cameras.  You're forced to make decisions to progress the story, although in a bit of hamfisted design, the developers obscure a lot of the readily available information you would have just to make the game more "interesting". 

The game is a very dry computer operation simulator where you're stuck using a fake web browser to plod through the tedious game, copying text and clicking on this and that.   I'm sure there's a "watching paint dry" simulator on Steam and it would be just as engaging.  Bonus points for the sheer irony of a game about big brother asking you for your email address so they can spam you and collect data on you.  That kind of dodginess is completely reprehensible, so even if the game was actually any good, I still wouldn't recommend it to make sure the developers are getting the message.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I played this game through once, and am surprised to read so many positive reviews, especially about the witing and characterisation which was weak, cliched and overall, spoilt my sense of immersion. 


I felt railroaded by this game- especially by your "advisor" who is constantly interrupting with inane nonsense. I rarely felt as though my choices seemed to matter. More so at the end, but by then I'd already resigned myself to the fact that this was an experience, not a game. 


The story itself was fine, and I like the general idea and premise of the game- putting you in the role of the investigator, making decisions which would cause the lives or deaths of the people you were investigating in, what must be seen as, a morally dubious way. 

The problem is, I never really did feel as though I was investigating, because for at least the first two days the game completely spoon feeds you, and feels as though nothing you do matters- the course of the story is inevitable. I don't mind being railroaded, but the game should at least have the illusion of choice. Every "data chunk" you upload causes something else to beep, leading you to the next. There is very little true decision making till the last day. 

Another problem is the extremely weak cast of characters who are all based on familiar and unimaginative stereotypes: the rebellious rich girl, the arrogant rockboy agintant, the foriegn professor with a mysterious past. The stereotypes might have been passable if it were not for the atociously written dialogue, which felt more like a high school drama conducted entiely by people with sub-par IQs. I found myself disliking all the characters and being irritated by the dialogue which so clearly served an agenda to ilucidate parts of the plot, instead of giving any sense of them being real people with real motivations. 

I also found the constant interruptions, the slow type speed of the conversations to be obnoxiously aggravating. The "assistant" rarely says anything of actual worth, and when taking data chunks in mid-conversation I really wish I could have switched him off, or the developers had limited his appearence. I also found the way that all new or unread data pinged up and highlighted in red meant that I almost never needed to think. I am sure that you could complete this game in a foriegn language just by clicking where the game told you, without understanding a single word of what's written. 

Now, having said all of this, I bought the game on sale and it's cheap. 5 hours of play time for £3.50- I guess there is a limit to what you can expect a studio to produce for that sort of budget. I'm pleased I didn't pay £7 for it though. 


Overall I think it's a poor handling of a great concept, and thus a wasted opportunity.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Orwell is a fresh new take on the visual novel game format. The game UI immediately immerses the player, placing you squarely in the driver seat as you try to unravel a bombing plot and pursue justice... but for whom?[/h1]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
You take on the role of a government surveillance cyber-investigator. Your task is to get into a person’s life through their social media, bank accounts, phone taps and chat messages. Drag and drop important bits of information (data chunks) into the ORWELL interface to upload these bits of data to form dossiers and help your supervisor inform the local authorities. 

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Evocative Experience[/u][/b]: 
Almost immediately, you’ll be oriented into the role of a cyber surveillance investigator and the stakes don’t get much higher than trying to unravel a terrorist plot. This game will make you *[b]feel[/b]* things and think about morality. 

[*][b][u]Novel UI [/u][/b]:
I think the UI is definitely the best part of the game, as it is designed in such a way to evoke the feeling of using some official piece of government software. Most of your interactions are in the form transcribed phone conversations, chat logs and browsing “online” content. 

[*][b][u]Art Style[/u][/b]:
The pixelated, somewhat-cartoony photos of people and places creates the perfect balance of reality and surreality. Probably for the best, as the game’s primary focus is to get you thinking about the heavy moral issues related to a surveillance society, as depicted by the game’s very Orwellian world. 

[*][b][u]Music[/u][/b]: Almost invisible, but ever present, the music stylings accented the drama perfectly. 
[/list]

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Lack of Visual Information[/u][/b]: 
A significant part of this game is reading text. Which you then choose to upload to Orwell or ignore (depending on the context of the circumstances and your personal value system).  

However, there were several times when I literally could not continue the game because the next event had to be triggered by me uploading some [b][u]some very specific, but unknown[/u][/b] piece of data. This created a situation where I would upload more info than I wanted to, just in an effort to trigger the next cutscene. 

Rather than guessing, it would have been nice if the designers could have implemented a color system or some other way to indicate what data was tied to progressing the story. I suppose the current implementation is more true to life, but it lessened my sense of agency when I would upload some seemingly innocuous data and suddenly my supervisor would dm me with a new break in the case. 

[*][b][u]File Organization[/u][/b]: 
By the end of the game, there are dozens of pages of fictitious files and documents to sift through... and the game did NOT make that task much easier. Could I get some bookmarks, please?

[*][b][u]RAILROADING[/u][/b]: 
So, I won’t say much here out of respect for spoilers, but suffice it to say that the design choices made in the game make it very clear how the developers feel regarding the subject matter. This bias in design limited the scope of user choice and the kinds of endings you can get. It would have been very interesting to have a greater variety of outcomes. It would have also worked to underscore the sense of user agency that they’d worked so hard to create in the first place.

[*][b][u]Short Length [/u][/b]: 
I’ve finished 2 complete playthroughs at 11 hours... which, given the minimalism of the graphics, seems extremely short and makes the current price of $9.99 a bit pricey.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Overall a very interesting and unique experience that I mostly enjoyed. However, because of the political nature of the game and the railroading embedded by the developers, I don’t think I’ll be buying any DLC any time soon, nor would I recommend the game at its current price of $9.99.

I really enjoyed Papers, Please.  I really enjoyed Beholder.  The "authoritarian minion simulator" is a really interesting game concept, and I wanted to like it, but Orwell just bored me.

It should be picking up clues to things that should go together, but gameplay is all highlighted drag & drop.  And thus I found myself not really caring.

It doesn't help that the drag & drop simulated internet is just enough of a facsimile to remind me I could be doing this on the real internet and it would be easier (albeit dead internet making it slightly harder in 2026).

You could quite literally start an X account and start reading posts by (let's see if my review makes it to being posted now!) Nick Shirley about mass fraud in the US or Rupert Lowe about mass... problems... in the UK and look for crimes actually being committed or covered up, then go and look at the names/places/groups in the reports they put out and start doing your own investigative work and start posting publicly available but little-known connections as you find them... and it would be both meaningful and less boring.  You wouldn't be an authoritarian minion, you'd just be someone doing basic investigative citizen journalism (or wonky tisming), but it's just finding connections.  Every "this you?" tweet where someone researches a political/celebrity timeline to find contradictory positions is more interesting that Orwell.

And that's why Orwell is weak.  Rather than go "huh, what's out there", it prompts the next link on a fake web, with things to drag and drop, over and over.

I wanted to like it, but found the story not hooking me in, the gameplay a tedious, railroading copy of the real internet, and overall just bleh.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell was an enjoyable, but very flawed game. I struggle with recommending it to anybody, because I can't imagine a particular audience falling in love with it. Gamers looking for a great narrative may find Orwell's offerings lacking, as I have. Gamers who are fans of the works of George Orwell may get what they're looking for, but as a fan myself I find the game's vision lacking. George Orwell's works were a denouncement of totalitarianism, yet his most well-known fictional books were either set in the real world or clearly based on real events and people. Orwell the game instead opts to take place in the wonderful setting of "The Nation" in which "The Party" exercises total control in a fictional world.

While the setting certainly lacks creativity, I was pleased to see that the plot and characters of the game improved as time passed. Orwell places the player as a worker for a state surveillence system looking for the perpetrator of a series of terrorist bombings. The player is tasked with reading various articles, profiles, and personal conversations and sending this information to the authorities within The Nation's government. This sounds more interesting than it plays out, however. In the beginning I was given a suspect who was very clearly not the bomber. I resented my superior for being so brainless for assuming they were responsible. While this suspect inevitably had some connections with people who actually did know more about the bombings, I was frustrated that I had to investigate the suspect in the first place. The gameplay also lacks for imagination. While I enjoyed reading some of the articles and the suspect's internet profiles, conversations, and e-mails, the text that you upload is already pre-determined. It ultimately boils down to a scavenger hunt. There are some choices to make things interesting. Sometimes you will have to chose between two pieces of data to upload to the authorities, as there may be conflicting data. Sometimes this decision is a moral one, and others it's more based around what the player things is more accuracte information. There are even a few times where uploading too much information will lead to unforeseen consequences. Regardless, for the most part the gameplay is very linear and will ultimately turn off many gamers. The gameplay gets more interesting in the final chapter when the uploads you can make are limited and the pressure is heightened, yet this improvement comes too little, too late.

Orwell is a game I want to love and there are moments of quality within. The general conclusion to the story was pulled off fairly well and there are consequences for chocies that many probably would not have anticipated being held accountable for. The characters and their interactions amongst each other are far more engaging than the uncreative setting. I hope for the sequel the developers be more bold with their setting, their message, and ultimately make the gameplay more interesting for a wider audience.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I just finished this game. I like many of the latest reviews received this as part of a humble bundle. Unlike many of the reviewers I am no stranger to the concept of interactive fiction. As such I cannot say "WOW so unique." This game has many elements I found fascinating, and indeed I played through the whole thing in one go, a very do-able task. I think there are many things that would make me recommend it, but there are two glaring holes that I think bring it just shy of a general recommendation. I can say this, If you have never played an interactive fiction game, and the plot sounds intriguing, buy it. It is worth ten dollars. If you got it in a humble bundle or something similar, play it. You will have an entertaining few hours. If you do not fall in to either of those two camps I would recommend a pass. 

The good - 
Plot- Everything to do with the plot is great. The characters are interesting, and they do to some degree develop. The world feels complete and well rounded, The plot is where this game shines, as it should be as interactive fiction lives and dies by the plot. 
The interface - For the most part is pretty solid. There are few idiosyncrasies. The one glaring hole is the need for a few hot-keys, if only Enter and ESC, would make this much easier on the wrists, but it is as a whole soundly usable. 

The bad - For the bad I will go in to detail as to hopefully explain my point of view fully to the Devs.  There is at least one more season planned, and I would love to play it. Perhaps the Devs will hear this feedback and consider it. Before I continue though, if you have already thought “I kinda want to play this game,” do it and forget the ramblings of an old gamer. 

Choice - If the plot is what an interactive fiction game lives and dies by then choice (or for that matter the illusion of choice) is what allows it to breath. In Orwell the idea of choice dies very quickly, and never returns. There are several pivotal moments which finds the player, through the narrative, put in a position to make a pivotal choice. All the relevant characters are obviously pointing at you and saying you decide. I never really felt like there was any choices to be made. Either The player is not given enough context to understand the consequences of that choice, in these cases you are just blindly choosing one of two options and made to accept the consequences. Or you cannot progress until you make the choice. 

At the heart of this, in my opinion, is the engine for which you as the player progress through the narrative. You are told at the very beginning of the game that you cannot progress until you have uploaded certain information. Which pieces of information allows for progression is up to the game. The premise of games like this in which it is up to the player to provide or not provide information to the antagonist is a great juxtaposition to make the player feel invested, and in many cases responsible for the consequences levied on the characters in the narrative. Games like “Papers Please” and “Beholder” levy this mechanic very well. In Orwell you cannot progress without giving the Antagonist certain information. This kills the illusion of choice, and make the rest of the narrative lose it's bite. Because I cannot NOT provide certain information the consequences are not my fault. The game made me do it. Especially in those moments where you have several data points you can give, and you need to choose between them, but if you choose wrong the game does not go forward, you end up throwing whatever data points at the wall, even those bits of data you do not want to provide, in order to get the game to continue. 

I realize why it was written this way. You cannot write a narrative which has ALL possibilities. So in order to move forward you need the player to trip certain triggers. An elegant way around this in my opinion would be to allow the information to be presented in "real time." This allows the narrative to continue while allowing the player more of a choice in the way it unfolds. I think this would greatly improve the impact of the game. 

The Twist - (mild spoiler warning) 
If you have read this far then I doubt this will really be a spoiler, but just in case, you have been warned.


There is a twist at the end. All good who-done-it's have them. This is no exception. My issue with the twist at the end of Orwell dove tails in to the idea of choice. There is no way you the player, let alone the character you play in the game, could predict it. There are no data points that I found that will allow you to discover the twist in game. Therefore it feels arbitrary. Once again the narrative loses impact because it does not feel like the player could intercede. The game is going to do what it is going to do and you are just pulled along to see what happens. that is what novels, TV shows, movies, and comic books are for. In fact I could see this story being a great Rashamon-Style comic, but as an interactive fiction I think this game falls flat. 

Summery - In summation I think if you are interested in games as an art form, or are just curios about what happens in this particular narrative, then this is worth while. I look forward to see if any of these issues are fixed in the next chapter. I do not regret my time "playing" this game. but I think in the end, The impact of the events was greatly blunted by the mechanics with which the narrative is presented. That seems a shame to me as the story could be quit impact-full if only the illusion of choice was maintained through out. In a narrative the promise of the premise is key, 
"Only the information you provide will be seen by the security forces and acted upon. You decide what gets seen and what does not, influencing how the suspects will be perceived." 
and this narrative missed that promise.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Unfortunately I didn't enjoy Orwell at all. Admittedly, it's been a sponatenous purchase, done out of sheer curiosity to see what the fuzz is all about.

But instead of a dystopian thriller, blending story and gameplay together with an innovative user interface, I got quite a dull experience.

Actually Orwell isn't a game at all, it's rather a semi-interactive story which simply progresses together with the text snippets you highlight  ("upload"). To make things a bit more interesting, your fictional self is supposed to participate in a surveillance and data mining program which observes persons and evaluates their behavior. You do that by browsing through social media profiles, reading blogs, newspapers, looking at photos and following text chats.

Noticed something? Yes, it's basically down to reading. The whole game could have been perfectly realized via a website, there is basically only a minimal amount of graphic assets involved. Now while that might work out for a well written game, it unfortunately fails for Orwell.

The story line tries to explore the important question of privacy, civil liberties and how social media and data mining can lead to their erosion, especially in light of an ubiqitous fear of terrorist acts.

But whoever wrote Orwell did it so heavy-handedly, that you quickly feel like you're stuck in a school lesson, with the teacher dancing around the obvious answer, because he thinks it's too complicated for you to understand it right away.

Even worse, while you might even find the person you follow being an interesting character, making you feel invested in how your actions will affect their life, you are constantly delayed by the process of gathering key information which will trigger the next story snippet.

And no, it's not interesting to browse through some fictional website, filled with trite and shallow pseudo-philosophical ramblings, in order to find that little piece of incriminating information which will suddenly prompt your supervisor to announce the next story progress ("she's a suspect, let's wiretap her / she's guilty, I am sending in the force with an arrest warrant). 

Actually it's quickly making you search for the next key snippet, dragging it to the upload window, just to rinse and repeat with another source you'll be presented with.

So bottom line, while playing Orwell I wondered what I am actually doing here.

If I want to have a linear story, presented (mainly) via text, guess what? Yes, I'll read a book. The benefit of doing so is that it's very probably better written, more accessible and I don't need to stare at a screen.

If I want to play a game, I will play a game. But then I expect something to actually utilize the manifold ways of presenting a story and of including me, the player (not reader), in its progress. (And yes, I actually play some classic text-adventure now and then.)

Orwell is neither the first nor the latter. It's an experiment which seems to aim high, but soon falls flat in its core design. After an hour I had enough. I'm not feeling invested or intrigued to continue at all, so Orwell will join the forbidden crypt of mistakes somewhere in the forsaken depths of my library.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought Orwell (on sale) expecting a sort of 1984 screens, eyes, with wiretaps everywhere. What I got was a message pop up game with a pretty compelling story. In that sentence, I just described the whole review. If you didn't get it - keep reading!

They say it's wrong to assume, and definitely after playing this, it's wrong to make assumptions sometimes. If there is a demo available, try it! This one didn't have it, and it was on sale - so I went for it. The [b]story[/b] is pretty good and well thought out, and has some serious twists and turns as it progresses. The characters are interesting and the game does a good job to keep the player guessing. The [b]gameplay[/b] revolves around making decisions on what to upload to "Orwell" (or the computer that connects all the dots) to decide the fate of the citizens that are being investigated. Basically. a text-rich game. Once a decision is made things get set in motion, very quick. During a specific period in the game I had the habit of uploading everything... just be careful what is deemed important! Someone may wrongly get arrested. 

The [b]visuals and graphics[/b] are very easy on the eyes. However, if you're someone who likes when the screen changes every once in a while, this might not totally be up your alley. The game consists of three or so main screens. The first is a headline type screen. This screen lets the player browse the web for interesting information they may come across. The second screen allows the player (working for Orwell) to listen in on live conversations or messages. The third screen is a computer hacking screen in which the player has access to a suspects computer. The game does a good progression to introducing the player to what is going on. The [b]sounds and music[/b] are pretty decent. There are moments in the game where the music will slam and something dramatic will happen. The sounds are alright and there is no live voice to the characters. I imagine being a small developper that can be hard to do, but the text does a decent job delivering a story. I'm not a text sort of gamer (my friend bought me Disco Elysium, I'm sure it's great, but just don't have the patience to play it), this game did catch my attention for a while though.

Why the negative review? If I had to warn my past self, I would advise my past self not to buy it. It's an awesome story, there are cool things that happen, but I feel indifferent to the game. I went down a mystery and I was put on the edge. Not enough for me to really like the game. If you like text based games and something that's a little different on Steam, or even mystery, decisions, and consequences... and especially if this game is on sale, I'd say definitely give it a shot. For me, I had a little fun. That's about it. It is sort of similar to Papers Please; Orwell is a little more linear to one story line. There are branches, but limited. The ending though, was definitely, as some would say, dope.  

This game has a story with a real lesson for the future. Would be interesting to see a new version of this game with more options and new tools to use.

review_text_raw:
This game is one of the few I don’t really feel I can fall down on either side. Ultimately, I felt I should mark it as unrecommended because I couldn’t bring myself to give it a thumbs up, and steam doesn’t have a ‘meh, its ok I guess’ option.

The story is, literally as it is titled, an Orwellian style, drama, I guess. Unfortunately the railroading detracts from the telling. 

The game play is actually pretty good and quite well done. As an investigator you’re expected to dig up as much information as you can regarding suspects in a terrorist attack, and then use their connections and the information gleaned to unpick what occurred and who is responsible, with the ultimate aim of preventing another attack. It is actually the limitations that are forced upon you to ensure you don’t get lost, combined with the multitude of ‘coincidences’ and other sloppy writing that only drives the story in a railroaded direction that bring the whole thing down.

Pros:
The game is easy to play, for the most part allows you to take your time reading the information and make your decision. The way the information is presented is also easy to digest and use. 
The characters are each unique and seem quite well thought out with their own motivations and histories. They also have an interesting dynamic that shows the growth, depth, and fading of their friendship as natural friendships have done.


Cons: 
The game opens with a single character to investigate, while that makes sense from a tutorial point, it doesn’t from a story point. This then focus and railroading leading to a contrived conclusion full of plot holes and excuses kinda ruins the game.
The system showcases a really interesting idea for ways to gather and profile information, monitor suspects, and use what you learn to further an investigation. Then it doesn’t let you do it, restricting what you can see to only a tiny window. It makes for a surveillance system that can’t watch anything.
Tying in to the above, we have so much information on the characters, but can’t utilise any of the information we would undoubtedly be able to access as law enforcement. Once again it felt like an artificial restriction, which was most frustrating.

Suggested improvements:
A skip dialogue button. Most of the few hours I’ve racked up were waiting for conversations to end.
Allow the system to access some of the surveyed individual’s data and build the puzzle environment that way.
Allow us to use the system in the ways we feel fit, not just the way that gives the narrative held.
For the love of god, let us investigate more people, more red herrings. Let us be the ones to cross off people from the lists, let us be the ones that decide what’s worth pursuing. 

Overall Recommendation:
This game has so much potential as a story driven and person centred hook. Especially for people who enjoy info hunts or detective style games. I can see it being really expandable with so many story options.
I think if you like that kind of game, this will scratch an itch for you.
But I can’t recommend it in its current state. As it is it comes off negatively and that just spoils all of the good things about it.
